I was actually one of the translators for this game and was promised a free copy of it upon returning the .txt file. It's in the game right now, I spent hours upon hours writing it and when sending an email to the developer, I received no reply for weeks. Decided to buy it however due to having to wait for it for approx. 2 years.

The concept is brilliant, yet simplistic. For those who love maps and history but don't enjoy the militaristic aspect of HOI4 and EU4, it seems like THE one. However, the developer gave up on updates, failed to interact with a loyal fanbase for months and treats the people who poured hours into helping him no respect.

Ignoring the background info, the game itself isn't terrible. The idea behind it was revolutionary I would say but fell short.

I have played this game for 30 now, so i have some experience in how the game works, and what you can do with it. So now i have made some changes to my original review, based on the things i saw in the game.

Two things to keep in mind with this game:
- it's just released, so a lot can still be added and changed
- The first Age of Civilizations was a mobile app. That's where the core of this game comes from. That said, having played the mobile game for a bit, this game a looking way better than the previous one. But still, this game also is getting an android version, which limmits the possiblities: you need to make sure phones can handle the game.

What is this game you ask?
It's a turn based grand strategy game. You control a nation within a scenario (scenario's currently in the game have the timeframe 600-2018). While controlling your nation you have control over its economy, technology, diplomatic relations and military. You can go to war and take over the world.

Many people that knew about this game being released got hyped because of the many different possibilities this game has to offer. It's main feature is the 1440 world map. With this scenario this game might become a competition for Europa Universalis IV. Would i compare this game to EU4? Yes and no. I don't think it is fair to compare Age of Civilizations II to that game. This game was made by 1 man, while EU4 has a whole team behind it. This is a turn based game, EU4 is real time. Does that mean this game is bad? certainly not! But it might be a little bit on the simplistic side for fans of the Paradox grand strategy games like myself. Many of the diplomatic features that are in EU4 are also in this game. That's good, although the competence of the AI is questionable. I do have hope for it though. When the game released the AI almost never declared any wars. Now (only a few weeks later!) there has been an AI update, where you can set the AI up to 400% aggressiveness. It is safe to say the AI is now more than capable to start wars. And fighting the wars is where the AI shines the brightest. I watched the AI play in spectator mode, and it is very enjoyable to see two nations going back and forward trying to invade each other. Unfortunately the AI for now isn't very good in diplomacy. It does make trade deals, asks for military access, and it loves improving relations with everyone, but it almost never makes alliances. I watched 1000 years of AI only and there were only ~ 5 alliances all including 1 province nations only. Does that mean allying is impossible? No the player can do it, and i have seen the AI accept my requests, but it doesn't make alliances on its own.

The way war works is a bit too simple for me. Do you have the superior numbers? then you win. Yes you can build a fort and win with inferior numbers, but really what misses in this game is some campaign strategy. EU4 doesn't have manual battles, but the terrain and placements of forts makes the warfare strategic in that game. Here you just smash your stacks into your enemies province, and cross your fingers your enemy has less troops than you. You might say: not knowing how many troops the enemy has makes wars a constant challenge. And yes i was surprised to see my 1200 men of Ottomans get wiped out by 1500 Albanians. But not knowing, not being given the chance to make strategic decisions does not make wars fun.

What about the Graphics and UI? the UI is a bit hard to figure out. I had to click around for minutes to find the screens i wanted to use. But it's all there, and grand strategy games aren't known for their good UI. Remember the endless amounts of screens, sliders and information that only pops up when you hover over it in Victoria 2? It is a real mess though. Yes there is an easy map mode button, that gives you most of the information you need, but there still are many other screens you just have to find yourself? remember i said terrain doesn't have effects? apparently it does. But good luck finding that one small button on the lower right corner where you can see the terrain in the selected province.

AI: The AI works best in warfare. It likes taking risks and sending small stacks far into enemy territory. This results in really enjoyable to watch AI only wars where the war turns around multiple times when an advancement gets stopped. When the game released the AI almost never declared wars. But in one of the many updates the game had over the last two weeks after launch the AI got fixed in this perspective. There even is a slider that lets you set the AI up to 400% aggressiveness.
Conclusion: It's a mixed bag, but still mostly positive. There are lots of bugs, the UI isn't good, and the warfare is a bit simplistic. It is really enjoyable. The 1 more turn mentality certainly applies to this game. Comparing this game to EU4 seems a bit unfair. If anything it's more like turn based Europa Universalis III (yes 3) light. That last point might actually be a good thing though. The game is really small, only a few hundred MB, and the requirements are so low even my University laptop that can't run Rome Total War is running it with no problem! I think this game getting its mobile release will be huge. Because while compared to popular PC grand strategy games it might lose, this game will be revolutionary on android! All those terrible free to play strategy games where you just move your troops around with no strategy or diplomacy? expect them to have a massive drop in users!

Do i advice buying this game? Yes certainly! It's only €5,- so what are you waiting for!

Age of History 2 (formerly: Age of Civilizations 2) is a great game to get into the genre. This game is a strategic in-between to the extremes of Paradox games like HoI4 and the board game RISK. It's also a game with many customization options that are easily accessible. For example, if you have an issue with a formable nation requiring too much land, there's a way to change it. You can also make your own start dates, your own countries, your own leaders, etc. As a single player experience, it is absolutely incredible that one individual made this game by himself. While, yes, this is a mobile game port, it's a REALLY GOOD mobile game. It deserved being put on PC just as much as Polytopia.

Unfortunately, multiplayer is heavily lacking. The only way to play with multiple people is with a "Pass and Play" system, which works on mobile fine I guess, but for PC it's terrible. While there is a Steam workshop, trust me when I say it's not anywhere CLOSE to the mods this game has. Because of that, playing many will require a lot of troubleshooting. That applies to making maps for the game as well. It's possible, but requires an external program, a lot of trial and error, and knowing what files need to be edited. The game would benefit heavily from having a map creator built-in, but that is unlikely to happen anytime soon.

The biggest issue, though, is how buggy this game is. It certainly takes some getting used to, but while most can be avoided when you get the hang of things, some will pop up every time you play the game. Recently, the dev seems to be taking interest in doing some bug fixes, but they're slow to come out and sometimes it just doesn't fix anything. If relations with other nations reset to 0 after turn 1000, or the names go completely bonkers, or the screen starts randomly flashing, or you can't even get every achievement, you're simply just gonna have to deal with it for now. If you don't buy it because it's buggy, I can't blame you.

HOWEVER, if you are thinking about buying this game, I think you absolutely should. It isn't a perfect game, but if you only care about single player, this game is worth more than its price point would even indicate. Those flaws are very outweighed by the game's positives. You buy this game to create scenarios with little effort compared to many other games. You buy this game to create an empire without having to learn thousands of in-game systems. You buy this game to do WHATEVER you want to do. This game will fall out of many's favor as they begin to prefer other more complicated, less buggy games, but personally I think this is a grand first step into playing strategy map games.

UPDATE: I have reviewed AoH3 in my own review, so no real mention here. Everything above still applies, and I still think this will be a good first step strategy game after RISK.

Also, the original Age of Civilizations is mobile only. Since it doesn't exist on Steam, here's a bonus review within this review: Don't play it. Don't bother playing it using something like BlueStacks or somehow finding an older phone to play it on. It's just a worse AoH2. If you want a similar experience but better in AoH2, turn on Age of Civilizations mode on the map ported from the original game. (world map but less provinces) Now you won't have terrible UI and be forced to use touchscreen controls with a mouse! Joy!

There's a lot of potential here, but there are also numerous bugs that mean I can't recommend the game in its current incarnation. From what I can tell from the forums here and on the dev's website, he has made nothing more than token gestures promising to provide fixes. However, since announcing imminent fixes many moons ago, he seems to have absconded and started working on another project instead. When it comes to this game, the dev is conspicuous by his absence.

Given that the game isn't likely to be fixed, I would suggest that you stay clear rather than rewarding that kind of attitude and business practice. While there are some workarounds suggested for some for the bugs, such as abandoning a province and then recapturing it the same turn to stop the economy tanking, fixing the bug would be a much better approach. There's also no guarantee you won't be hit by other game-breaking bugs for which there is no workaround.

So in the absence of any hope of these bugs (that seem to affect lots of players) being fixed, I'd suggest you stay away, and treat any subsequent releases by the same dev with caution. Yes, it's a one-man show, so some leeway is fine. No one expects overnight fixes. But a certain amount of pride in one's work and a desire to deliver quality should be the foundation of any software product.

The reviews are generally positive, and that's because there's a great game here waiting to get out. It's a shame seeing it being left to rot in a semi-finished state. And while 5 smackeroos isn't a particularly painful amount to write off, you can still vote with your wallet and say no to dodgy devs who abscond leaving behind a half-finished game.

Age of History II looks simple at first, but once you get into it, you realize how deep it actually is. The map covers the entire world and you can play as pretty much any country, from ancient times to modern day. Whether you want to build a peaceful empire through diplomacy or crush your enemies with military power, the game gives you that freedom.

The best part is how flexible it is. You can rewrite history in endless ways: make small nations rise into global powers, recreate old empires, or completely change the outcome of major wars. Every campaign feels different, and there’s always another strategy to try out.

It’s not perfect. The interface can feel clunky at times, and the game can be overwhelming if you’re not used to grand strategy. But once you get the hang of it, it’s incredibly addictive. Hours disappear without you realizing it.

If you enjoy history, strategy, and the idea of controlling the fate of nations, Age of History II is absolutely worth it.

Do I recommend it?
Yes, especially for strategy fans who like having total control over world history.

Strategic, easy to learn, easy to make scenarios, and creativity explodes once you get the hang of it. You'd go from playing as Soviet Union, and taking over the world, to playing as a small weak country, and still dominating the world!

The game is rather quite fun, and it's kind of a more casual version of the Paradox games.
The recent name change though, oh good lord. It doesn't do the game good, as it's about countries, and is not about following history. It's like calling a Fort a Field, A fort is well defended and commonly hard to breach, A field otherwise, is wide open to walk through. The original name "Age of Civilizations II" is much better of a representation, and does it good.
Still, please play this game if you enjoy this Genre.

Edit:
This game has not aged the best, lets establish that. This game is still fine but has not been updated in years, and still has a surprising amount of bugs. I'm not going to say you shouldn't try this game, but before you do please accommodate your mindset to it having aged without much maintenence.

This is one game that I play a lot and I enjoy, the main idea is good and well-executed but unfortunately, I can't recommend this game because it has a lot of problems for someone who wants to play it a little bit deeper.

[h1]Pros[/h1]

The game is cheap and all the music is just amazing and fits the ambiance. Even though the main strategy for this game is easy to learn, the way how the game works is what makes it special.  You can visualize your relationships and have a clear understanding of who is your enemy and who is your friend. Everything is logical and when you understand the game, you will have a good time messing around with the stats and economy of your country. 
My favorite part of this game is how dynamic the wars are and how tricky they can get. You have a lot of options in-game like changing your type of government, moving your capital, creating a vassal, changing your country's name, and other things. In-game, you have an entire "window" with tables and graphics where you can see how is your country compared with others and it is amazing.

[h1]Neutral[/h1]

The game's interface is not bad, but it could be better, specifically the menu and it can get confusing when you are changing advanced options. The game gets so confusing that when I was exploring all the options and tools I ended up changing accidentally the population growth of some provinces and there was no option to make it all default again. After that, I had to reinstall the game.

[h1]Cons[/h1]

Now, it seems that this game is awesome, and the idea is amazing, but it lacks the basics.
The game is buggy in a way that it can easily destroy some progress, or you will have to re-open the game to play again. I will say some bugs:
[list]
    [*]One time the game interface simply died, there were only flashy colors. I couldn't do anything and I had to close the game, losing some progress;
    [*]Sometimes, randomly, your units simply perish, and it can affect your game badly;
    [*]If you annex a country and they have units on water, there is a chance of the units stay in that position forever;
    [*]On long games (+1000 turn) there is a small change of all countries' opinions reset to 0 and you can't improve your relationship.
[/list]
Probably there are more bugs that I simply don't remember right now. 
This game needs a real Steam Workshop. If you want more scenarios or mods you have to go to the creator forum and download those via other links. After that, you have to put the mod files by yourself into the game files. All of this is just dumb considering that Steam created the Workshop to made all of this much easier.
I bought the game almost 2 years ago and, as far as I remember, there was only "one big update" that changed the name of the game, deleted all my civilizations (like 300 hours gone, thank you), and only added 1 map, that honestly, I think no one asked for it, with some scenarios, while after that there still bugs. I'm not saying that the developer is not working hard, I just think that if he can't handle all the work, he could maybe get some help, because, being honest, this game without bugs, and with the Steam Workshop implemented is worth a lot more than 5 euros.

Age of Civilizations II, simply put, is a game that is severely lacking in functionality.

These types of games are meant to offer a strategic aspect however there is no true strategy to speak of. War is just a numbers game - and not a smart numbers game with weapon values or supplies and such. It's essentially just "bigger number beats smaller number". Not to mention that you don't have options between infantry, tanks, warships, aircraft, etc. It's just "units". The worst part is that there are no front lines or anything like it. It's province by province, and even if you capture a nation's capital they don't capitulate. Chances are they're cutting off your route and instead taking out every single once of your own provinces turn by turn.

There is little in terms of depth of politics. There are no internal political goals. The most I found was trying to boost population. Foreign affairs is little more than pressing 'improve relations' or 'send insult' every time the timer finishes. Not only that, but they is little accuracy in terms of foreign policy, meaning that you get things like Canada and the UK or the USA and Puerto Rice going to war within the first 10 turns because reasons. I once tried doing a WWII scenario as the UK holding back the Axis and then had war declared on me by America for no reason. On top of all this there is no apparent goal aside from take over the entire map.

There is also no resource system to be heard of, instead replacing all of that with money. While the concept of having a treasury may sound interesting at first it's really non-intuitive because it's constantly trying to make money every turn while being strangled to death by "administration" or military upkeep, meaning that you have to wait for a large enough treasury before recruiting, leaving you vulnerable to attack,

Overall there is little strategy involved instead making it a game of "spam next turn enough to start recruitment."

There is also a lack of leaning resources. To my knowledge there is no wiki and YouTube tutorials are far and few between, making a mechanic or button that isn't obvious through it's name or description isn't the easiest to figure out.

However I will give the game credit where credit is due:

The Scenario Editor is a fairly easy to access way to make your own placements, meaning that if you want to "recreate" (In quotes because it's difficult to make anything play out accurately) certain sections of history or make your own custom countries and map placements easily. While not the most robust system it gets the job done.


In conclusion:

Age of Civilizations II is a very simplified version of Paradox Games such as HoI4, EU4, CK2, etc. I was rather disappointed with Age of Civilizations II after seeing what little it has to offer compared to Paradox games, however if you're looking for a dumbed down version of Paradox's offerings it's not awful for the price (especially when it's on sale) but if you want something with substance get a Paradox game.

I have been playing this game for a while so I thought I would post a review

First off, I do like this game. There are many scenarios to play throughout history and it is fun to expand you empire over hundreds of years. It is also very cheap and does not require a good PC which is very nice. unfortunately there are some problems that I have with the game (though most are small). 

There are some pretty annoying glitches in the game. It is not uncommon for some things like cities, castles or port icons to disappear requiring a reset of the game to get them back. The worst glitch I seen is one where all of your armies will despawn in between turn. This glitch is very common for me usually happening about 2 times per save. With how debt works in the game having your army dis appear has caused me to lose. Fortunately if you frequently save you can go back but it is still annoying. 

unfortunately leaders are immortal and city names do not reflect the year you play in. Also provinces are optimized for the modern day which creates some weird borders for past scenarios. The gameplay is also repetive with the larger amount of units winning but with defenders getting a defense buff. There is also not a lot of meaningful diplomacy which is disappointing.  

While I have spent a lot of this review going over negatives, I truly do find the game fun but I think it is important to highlight the issues the game has.

Unfortunately just a mobile game that tries to be every Paradox game in one despite making fun of Paradox games.

Completely abandoned by sole dev with several actually game breaking bugs still in the game, presumably features instead of bugs. Your game won't last more than 2k turns because if it does, your relations with other nations will break and this bricks your save because you cant declare war or do anything.

The AI is barebones and is often persuaded by 27 gold pieces that their "neighbor" from South America offered them to declare war on you, the player. Even though the south american nation is offering 27 gold to an AI in Europe. To declare war on you..
It feels designed to screw you, and only you, the player over.  These checks and bribes are all done in one turn as well, so you can 90% of the time savescum and just... not go to war with a bribed AI.

However, barring that, the game is incredibly easy to cheese after getting a slight grip of all the mechanics. It being turn based means you also have to micro tens of things in one turn for every turn you play, so every save just becomes a microfest that makes HOI4 multiplayer look like a silly spelling bee.

The game also crashes whenever it feels like it, so you better hope you had an autosave.
Age of History II also has a crippling lack of quality of life features. Colonization is easily the most egregious example: you have to manually colonize every province, which, let's admit it, gives you a lot of control over borders and how pretty your nation looks... but it's not fun when you HAVE to click 2 million times on vastly differing places, making it so you're in for actual carpal tunnel syndrome.

The ai also does not have any preprogrammed checks in peace deals like "will this be an enclave completely surrounded by someone else's land?" and so bordergore is the norm... prepare for a headache. And also, stronger AI nations sometimes chill out, letting small minors become stronger... there's just, nothing to be found here. Every AI is a speedbump for you to go over, some are stronger than others but they're still just speedbumps.

Diplomacy is also garbage with AI insulting you diplomatically, lowering your opinion and severing relations, to be frank, absolutely RANDOMLY. Even your own created puppets will insult you and if the relations go into the negatives, they'll suddenly start craving freedom, and declare it. There are more diplomatic options than, say, HOI4, but they all suck and only one is worth using: declare war. What does that say about this game?


The combat, which you will be experiencing for 90% of the game, is also just hot garbage. It's 100% "who has more numbers?" with a little bit of "well you're on a mountain so the enemy needs a couple more men to kill you" sprinkled on... but it is genuinely 99% of the time just a matter of having more men than the enemy.  There are also thousands of provinces ingame, which you will have to manually capture for a 'world conquest'... I never got farther than conquering a continent before I was either stopped from playing by the 2k turns bug or sheer boredom of knowing I'll beat anything through a war of economics anyway...

Recruitment is only possible on owned provinces, so have fun pushing deep into countries (you cant see how many troops an enemy has unless a tile has a watchtower) with your 3k men hitting the AI's 24k man stack and dying... resulting in the collapse of the invasion because you can't recruit in occupied territory.
Like, this game has one bad design decision after the other just everywhere.
Colonization is too accessible, with it being too easy for even minors to get colonies outside of Europe. Every game will have minors chill about and most likely go for anything that's neutral territory... so, Africa, America, Pacific, etc...

The game easily gets boring and tends to become a power fantasy. I do applaud that the game lets you choose what provinces/tiles to release puppets in and even lets you create your own puppets' flags but this isn't nearly enough to overcome the game's several flaws. In fact, this flag creation is a bit barebones with lacking symbols and flag backgrounds. The flag customizer itself is also janky.

While it is a "Lite Paradox Game" that's easy to pick up and have... well, 'fun' in heavy quotation marks, it's still just a bit too lite. It's a game that makes you want to think its not that shallow, that it has depth - but fails at it, and it shows. About as wide as a puddle, and as deep as one.

The game is buggy as hell
The start of every game is very good, you don't feel like eveything is being gifted to you. Obviously there are civilizations that are more difficult than others.
However the balance of civilization power is mostly given to their population. Economy, diplomatic relations and size practically don't matter at all.

Trade is messed up
There is this bug where if you trade 100 gold (which is nothing) to a civilization, you can make them go to war with whatever nation you can think of. There are other options to trade, like provinces, military access, defensive pacts, non-agression pacts, etc. But I haven't been able to trade with any of them, even when I'm the most powerful civilization of the game.

Civilization Power and Combat
As I said before, the power of a civilization comes from its population ONLY. More population means you can have many more armies or numbers because that's all they are on the map. An example of this is France and the British Raj in the 1936 scenario, this are two most powerful civilizations of the scenario. When playing, the British Raj proclaims independence from the British since they both have the same power, and thus it messes up the alliance between Britain and France which gives them both tremendouse power and making the unbeatable if you don't make them declare war to each other with the trade bug.

Combat is confusing. There are modifiers of terrain that affect how well your army does on certain terrains like mountains or deserts, but late in the game, they don't really matter that much since, by that point, armies are in the tens of thousands and these penalizations are unnoticiable.

Other weird bugs
When you are pretty far off in the game, this bug happens where all diplomatic relations between relations are set and stuck to zero, you can't improve or severe relations anymore.

Also it tends to happen very often that an economic cluster always happens, this means only one civilization in the game will start to pump a single province with money to improve its economy.

The goods
The colonization system is pretty good. It makes sense that in early game colonization is expensive and when you unlock more science points and time passes, it becomes cheaper. But you can't create vassals to administer said colonies because a British Raj scenario could happen.

The actual gameplay is very simplistic:
_______________________________
-Economy is basically just bigger economy=more money. The biggest issue I see with this is that in long games where you might want to roleplay smaller states just invest infinitely into their tiles and they get insane levels of economy. This is a huge issue in the 1440 start date with the HRE states. I've seen Ulm have like 60k economy which is absolutely insane for a "city state".

-Development just allows you to invest money into tiles easier and build economy more. It isn't really interesting.

-Taxation is always capped at a certain level and ideologies play an insignificant role in changing the rate you can tax at before your population hates you. So yeah Ideology is mostly just aesthetic.

-War is repetitive since its just whoever has a bigger unit stack that wins. There's no quality aspect and terrain has practically no effect in combat. Peace deals are super annoying since if you have a vassal they will actually take territory for themselves and mess up whatever plans you had for the land you just conquered. 

-War declarations are solely based on "opinion" where the lower the number the more likely you are to be declared on. Sometimes you'll have coalitions of nations declare war on you that make no sense. For example: a Japanese warlord, Poland, Tuscany, and whatever other random nation that hates you might declare war on you for no reason whatsoever other than that they all hate you. This can get annoying, really quickly.

-Assimilation is just click button, spend lots of money, and people happy in 50 turns.

-AI is dumb and will stay at war with another nation for a really, really long time until their enemy is usually completely beaten.

__________________

So yeah. I've spent around 2+ weeks of my life playing this game at the time of writing this. The game needs some work, but that doesn't mean you won't have fun with it. It's a fun thing to kill time with or when you want to create some custom scenarios and mess around in them. I enjoy it quite a bit.

The part of this game I've loved the most is the custom map and nation creator which is actually pretty fun to mess around with and make your own scenarios with. I've tried to script events into my scenarios as well, but there are some glitches with the scripting and some commands just don't work at all. In order to script a set peace deal it takes a great deal of effort and you have to hope to god that the AI doesn't make its own border-gore (which if you leave the game running for like 50 turns it will). So yeah if you want to try that go ahead, but scripting events has a learning curve and I still don't think I even fully understand it. It's just functional enough to script a decent start to a scenario if you want to.

Some general tips:
-Put AI aggressiveness at 50% (the lowest) for a more sane experience.
-if you want to annex all of the land you just conquered but you can't since you don't have enough war score, just vassalize the nation and lower your opinion of that vassal until you can demand annexation (they'll accept if your army is at least a bit bigger than theirs). Then release a vassal again and adjust the borders how you want.
-This game is all about population. If you have a large population, you can make big armies, which means you win.
-Play sandbox mode if you don't want to bother with money and just want to Role-play empire building. Sandbox also lets you end wars with AI instantly so it's a lifesaver if you want to avoid constant declarations.
-You can add your own formable nations and I recommend you do.
-If you script events into a scenario: DO NOT observe it as a spectator or else your events will break and you'll have to fix it manually.

[h1] A Europa Universalis Clone that Fails to Keep Interest [/h1]

Age of Civilizations II is a grand-strategy game very similar to Paradox's Europa Universalis. However, it ignores many of the complexities of such games, and instead favors a more simplistic approach focusing on charts and one-click playing. I would agree with the "easy to learn but hard to master" tagline for this, but when you get to that "mastering" point the game's flaws show through. The simplicity turns out to be this game's weakness, resulting in irritation when waging wars that turn into a "who can produce the most units the fastest" and rush before the other country can produce replacement units. The problem with the turn-based gameplay allows for the AI to rush undefended provinces and take them over in a turn, resulting in an annoying cat-and-mouse as each side produces limitless amounts of units each turn. The game plays out like a mobile one with poor graphics (the flags particularly) and the "zoom" can result in provinces being too close to each other to even see. 

The game does allow you to play various scenarios (some humorous ones like the Great Emu War (never forget) and the Football War turning hot). This can keep interest, but you realize that each scenario turns into the same boring, irritating gameplay as you slowly conquer the world. Diplomacy is on its worse end completely pointless as the AI rarely provides useful help, and there's little consequence for going ballistic. In the end, just get Europa Universalis IV if this is the type of game you want.

Age of Civilizations 2 is an attempt to make a turn-based version of Europa Universalis, but lacks the depth of even EU1, but has double the frustration.

AoC2 is not an easy game, but this is due to the game's 3 primary sins: Wars of Attrition, Terrible Economic Growth, and Erratic Diplomacy.

[b]Attrition:[/b] Battles annihilate both armies, and terrain is of minimal help.  Warfare thus becomes a matter of grinding bloody attrition which is to be avoided at all costs, where losing 3,000 men to defeat 2,500 entrenched defenders can be considered a "Victory" if you managed to gain the land.  If you expand your territory through war, for every 20,000 population you conquer, expect to lose 2,000 men and kill 2,000 enemies.  Your homelands can quickly get depleted of manpower which has no easy way to get replenished.  When stopping a naval landing, expect to lose 800-900 soldiers for every 1,000 you kill, and end with nothing to show for it but empty shores and empty treasuries.

[b]Economy:[/b]AoC2 likes to take things slow with growth.  Spend your 7500 starting treasury in your best province and be amazed as your income jumps by a whopping 50g/turn.  In AoC2, a 150 turn return period is considered a good deal.
Trying to regrow a population devastated by war isn't easy, because this is a matter of your national budget as well.  If you need more population, you have to spend gold on "Goods" in order to get it.  Trying to grow your population in order to boost your income though is a losing game, with gold spent on population growth needing about 500 turns to pay for itself.  No that's not a typo. 500.  I did the math.  Sometimes it can get as good as 250 turns!
The best growth I've seen has been Technology.  Researching the early tech levels has returns that take less than 100 turns, but tech costs quickly scale up with the levels.  These costs do not scale with the size of a nation though, so only the biggest/richest of nations can reach the highest tiers.

[b]Diplomacy:[/b] This is the most frustrating aspect of the game.  Diplomacy has a lot of options, but in practise it means desperately trying to hold onto allies while nations randomly hurl insults around to create chaos and war in the world.  If you have been insulted, all efforts to improve relations with that nation are suspended for the next 20-40 turns.  Once a nation dislikes you, there is basically nothing you can do to ever become friendly again.  Your only hope for peace and security is to focus all of your diplomatic efforts on a few strong nations from Day 1 and get them to like you enough not to throw insults faster than you can repair the damage.
For everyone else, you can expect grinding, pointless, suicidal wars.  And this is where the game becomes REALLY frustrating.

Did I mention all wars are wars of attrition?  Did I mention that [b]the AI will never accept a White Peace[/b]?  Do you think that these factors combined could result in AI nations spamming you with endless suicidal attacks that accomplish nothing but draining both your Manpower?  Because that happens.  Frequently.  Have fun getting stuck in pointless wars that had no reason to begin and are impossible to end.

[b]Conclusion:[/b] The game is "Hard" because your choices are between investing in an anemic Economy, or a meatgrinder  Battlefield, while you are facing opponents that will happily drag you down with them into the abyss.  "Winning" involves a careful diplomatic dance (and a little luck) so you can avoid wars against anybody who isn't already being torn apart by your neighbors.

[b]If you want a game where you try NOT to fight, and your investments yield NO RETURNS, and the world's population is destroyed as pointless warfare rages around you, then this is the game for you![/b]

DO NOT BUY THIS GAME

I'm not really a genre vet, as much as I try to be. But I don't think this is going to do the trick for those who are genre vets. This is almost akin to "my first Grand Strategy", something you could use to introduce newcomers thanks to its approachability and free-for-friends remote play hosted multiplayer. But I'd definitely not recommend it to people who play HOI4 or Crusader Kings to get their rocks off.

Balance is finicky - it took me a few goes to start winning a game on normal difficulty but then there was nothing in the entire game that could threaten me.

For some reason, starting unit counts are randomized, so I might get none and other nations get hundreds, restart, totally different setup even with identical nations. This is one of the more noticable way AI exploits the game in an asymmetrical way.

AI will throw themselves into a situation they can't win as if their programming tricked them into thinking it would work. Repeatedly. They're not really trying to outsmart you just throw numbers at you regardless of your own. They rarely split units, or reinforce smaller numbered forts. They almost always attack even when they should be on defense.

Tying movement points to construction building means you can't build as many things per turn as you could otherwise, and if gold excess is such a problem you need to artificially limit how much I can spend per turn, then lower how much gold is given out lol.

Regarding naval movements; units can enter islands from the sea but cannot enter the sea without a port. THERE ARE A LOT OF ISLANDS that are isolated territories so have fun building a port for every single one.

Regarding the game's says-on-the-tin-simplicity: It might be too simple. There's only four things you can do; build something, make or move units, fiddle with economy sliders, and (really REALLY barebones) diplomacy.

Another thing that annoys be is that if you select a territory, then click another, it'll try to move the units even if you didn't hit move. It's really annoying and makes it hard to skim through territories, which should be easy.

I dunno. It's a cheapy and might be fun to remote play with your friends, since there's only one copy needed it's the cheapest multiplayer grand strategy there is. But the simplicity, fiddliness and wonky difficulty makes it very difficult for me to recommend for solo play, but I found it a lot more approachable than HOI4 so, it has that going for it.

Age of History II is a very simplified version of Paradox games such as Hearts of Iron IV.

It's really fun for the first 5 hours, but then it becomes repetitive because it's almost impossible to lose—even on the hardest difficulty. The AI complexity doesn't change at all, you just have a harder time making money so you're an easier target. But being attacked can be avoided by just spamming "Improve Relations."

That's it, that's the entire game. It's just spamming buttons and colouring your map. The only reason why I currently have 50+ hours played is because of the formable nations (Italy ---> Rome), but even that gets old really fast considering how few of those formable nations there are. Some of the greatest and most infamous kingdoms and empires are even missing.

Not to mention this game hasn't seen a proper update since 2020, so there's plenty of annoying bugs such as your camera randomly jumping to the corner of the map, or the names of nations getting jumbled.

This game also loves to throw random declarations of war on you, even though the nations are worlds apart. Sometimes I can't even tell where the invading country is, because the game doesn't mark it. That way, all you can do when a speck of a nation attacks you, is watch in bafflement.

At the end of the day, Age of History II is a good game if you're scared by Paradox's complexity, but the cons outweigh the pros, and you will get bored really quick.
